# Introduction
This vignette uses text2vec and Stonybrook's novels dataset to create a classification and regression model to predict the likelihood of success for novels and other literary texts. The dataset and various approaches to creating a classifier are discussed in the original article "*Success with Style*" [@ashok_success_2013].

The authors of the original study chose to publish the raw data used for their dataset but did not publish the source code to their classifier. In the original study, the author's built a classifier using LibLinear SVM. They used a variety of approaches to transform text into "features" suitable for training a classifier. In this example, we make use of text2vec which, as its name implies, provides the tools to transform text into feature vectors.

```{r setup, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)
library(text2vec)
library(glmnet)
library(tools)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(devtools)

library(novels)

```
# The "novels" dataset
The novels dataset consists of `r dim(novels)[1]` entries. Some of the entries refer
to the same text file, e.g. in the case where a literary work belongs in more than one category (fiction and short story). For training, it's important that we only train on a given text once. In the entire dataset there are `r sum(novels %>% select(gutenberg_id) %>% duplicated)` duplicates.

Also, author's may have multiple works in the dataset. While we have a total of `r dim(novels)[1]` entries in the dataset, there are fewer authors `r length(unique(novels$author))`.

# Create training and test sets
```{r split, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
# Make response value an integer for AUC computation. Test to prevent
# confusion when rerunning code chunks.
if(class(novels$response) == 'factor') {
  stopifnot(novels$response == 'success' || novels$response == 'failure')
  novels$response <- as.integer(novels$response == 'success')
}
#
# Since this demonstration ignores genres and folds and trains with neither,
# we have to explicitly deduplicate the dataset. As noted elsewhere, a given
# text may appear more than once if it belongs to more than one genre. This
# dedup is scoped to training/prediction only -- the per-genre reporting
# further below re-expands predictions against novels::novels's full,
# un-deduped genre membership, rather than relying on whichever single
# genre happened to survive this dedup for a given book.
#
novels = dedupe_by_group(copy(novels::novels), "gutenberg_id")
setDT(novels)
indices <- createSplit(novels, seed = 2026L)
train = novels[indices$train]
test = novels[indices$test]
```

# Feature extraction
Create a text2vec iterator, vocabulary, vectorizer and document text matrix (dtm). The dtm represents the novels data set as trainable features.
```{r document-text-matrix, eval = TRUE, cache = TRUE, cache.extra = list(packageVersion("novels"), digest::digest(novels::novels))}
it <- novels::getIterator(train$text, train$title)
vocab <- novels::text2vocab(it, length(train$text))
vectorizer = vocab_vectorizer(vocab)
dtm = create_dtm(it, vectorizer)
```

# Normalization
Transform the dtm to an idf to normalize the data and make it machine learning friendly.
```{r tfidf, eval = TRUE, cache = TRUE, cache.extra = list(packageVersion("novels"), digest::digest(novels::novels))}
# define tfidf model
tfidf = TfIdf$new()
# fit model to train data and transform train data with fitted model
dtm_tfidf = fit_transform(dtm, tfidf)
```
```{r, echo=FALSE}
rm(dtm)
```

# Build classifier
Build a classifier using a generalized linear model (glm) with cross-validation (cv).
```{r classifier, eval = TRUE, cache = TRUE, cache.extra = list(packageVersion("novels"), digest::digest(novels::novels))}
glmnet_classifier = cv.glmnet(x = dtm_tfidf, y = train$response,
                              family = 'binomial',
                              alpha = 0.05,
                              type.measure = "auc",
                              nfolds = 5,
                              control = list(
                                thresh = 1e-5,
                                maxit = 1e4
                                ))
```

# Display AUC for the resulting model
Area under the curve (AUC) is a time-honored approach to evaluating the effectiveness of a model. Here we use the *glmnet* package to plot the AUC for different values of the control variable "lambda".
```{r plot-auc}
plot(glmnet_classifier)
```

# Evaluate test set
To understand the quality of our classifier, we want the model's best AUC result for both training and test data sets. We want AUC scores as close to 1 as possible, ideally over .9.

Although the test set rarely exceeds the training set results, we want a test set AUC result that is close to the training set AUC.
```{r eval-test-set}
classifier <- createPredictor(vectorizer, tfidf, glmnet_classifier)
# get a prediction for confusion-matrix consumers
test_results <- classifier(test) %>% classifyAt(threshold = 0.5)
# compute test_auc from test_results$probability
test_auc <- glmnet:::auc(test$response, test_results$probability)
train_auc <- max(glmnet_classifier$cvm)

# test_results has one row per unique book (test was deduped above), each
# carrying only whichever single genre survived that dedup. For per-genre
# reporting, re-expand each book's prediction against novels::novels's
# full, un-deduped genre membership -- a book belonging to both Fiction
# and Short Stories should get real credit under both, not just whichever
# one happened to survive the earlier training-focused dedup. The pooled
# "all" row further below still uses test_results directly, so no book is
# double-counted there.
test_results_by_genre <- test_results %>%
  select(-genre) %>%
  inner_join(novels::novels %>% select(gutenberg_id, genre), by = "gutenberg_id")
```
The classifier produces an AUC of `r sprintf("%02.2f", train_auc * 100)` on training data and an AUC of `r sprintf("%02.2f", test_auc * 100)` on test data.

```{r summarize-scores, echo = FALSE}
summarizeScores <- function(results) {
  results %>%
        mutate(
          author = toTitleCase(as.character(author)),
          title = toTitleCase(as.character(title)),
          prediction = novels::results2Text(prediction),
          response = novels::results2Text(response)
        ) %>%
        select(author, title, score, download_count, prediction, response) %>%
        arrange(desc(score))
}

prettyPrintScores <- function(results) {
  kable(summarizeScores(results) %>% head(n = 100)) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"))
}
```

# Some Test Scores for the Fiction Genre
Let's look at the relative scores for examples of fiction in the test set just to get a sense for how it performs.
```{r test-scores, echo = FALSE}
prettyPrintScores(test_results_by_genre %>% filter(genre == 'Fiction'))
```
# Define function to evaluate performance
```{r define-evalauate-performance-function}
evaluatePerformance <- function(results) {
  results %>% createConfusionMatrix %>%
      addInformationRetrievalMetrics
}
```

# Classifier Results by Genre
This table shows how the classifier performs for a given genre.
```{r, results-by-genre}
# Read from novels::novels directly, not the local (deduped, data.table-
# converted) `novels` variable -- the local one happens to still carry
# the full factor levels today, but that's incidental to how dedup and
# setDT() were implemented, not something this should depend on.
genres <- levels(novels::novels$genre)
resultsByGenre <- cbind(data.frame(Genre = c('all')), evaluatePerformance(test_results))
for(g in genres) {
  resultsByGenre <- rbind(
    resultsByGenre,
    cbind(
      data.frame(Genre = c(g)),
      evaluatePerformance(test_results_by_genre %>% filter(genre == g))
    )
  )
}
resultsByGenre %>% kable() %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"))
```
# Text2vec Performance Compared to Stony Brook EMNLP13
This table shows how the GLMNET / text2vec classifier stacks up to the results reported in the "*Success with Style*" article. The GLMNET column shows the performance of our classifier. The best per genre column shows the best result obtained by each of Sunnybrook's 15 models in each genre. The best overall column shows the performance of the best single classifier over all the genres. The n column carries over each genre's test-set book count from the table above -- worth weighing before trusting any single genre's number too far; a handful of books can swing a percentage a long way. Genres below the flagged threshold are shown in red.

The narrative below judges "meets or beats Stonybrook" against the best overall column, not the best per genre column. Best per genre reflects the best of 15 separately genre-tuned models; best overall is Stonybrook's own single classifier evaluated across every genre, the fair like-for-like comparison against this vignette's own single pooled GLMNET classifier. A genuinely per-genre GLMNET pipeline, comparable to best per genre on equal terms, is on the roadmap but not yet built -- until then, treat any gap against best per genre specifically as expected, not as evidence of a real shortfall.
```{r best-of-sunnybrook, echo = FALSE}

# Explicit mapping from this corpus's actual genre strings to the
# Success with Style paper's Table 1 numbers, independent of whatever
# order resultsByGenre's rows happen to come in. (This used to be built
# by zipping the raw number vector positionally against
# resultsByGenre$Genre, which broke once levels() started sorting
# alphabetically instead of matching the original corpus's directory
# order -- see project history.)
sunnyBrookAccuracybyGenre <- data.frame(
  Genre = c('all', 'Adventure', 'Detective/Mystery', 'Fiction', 'Historical Fiction',
            'Love Story', 'Poetry', 'Sci-Fi', 'Short Stories'),
  BestPerGenre = c(73.5, 84.0, 75.0, 75.0, 61.0, 82.0, 74.0, 76.0, 77.0),
  BestOverall  = c(73.5, 75.0, 75.0, 75.0, 58.0, 81.0, 72.0, 76.0, 77.0)
)

comparisonTable <- resultsByGenre %>%
  inner_join(sunnyBrookAccuracybyGenre, by = 'Genre') %>%
  mutate(GLMNET = Accuracy, n = Total) %>%
  select(Genre, n, GLMNET, BestPerGenre, BestOverall)

# Small-sample flag threshold, in test-set books. A judgment call, not a
# statistically derived cutoff -- worth revisiting if it ever matters.
small_sample_threshold <- 15

comparisonTable %>%
  mutate(n = kableExtra::cell_spec(
    n,
    format = "html",
    color = ifelse(n < small_sample_threshold, "red", "black"),
    bold = n < small_sample_threshold
  )) %>%
  kable(escape = FALSE, format = "html") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"))

```
```{r sunnybrook-narrative, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}
# Built from comparisonTable itself, not hand-typed -- this paragraph
# stays correct automatically as results change, rather than needing a
# human to remember to rewrite it every time the pipeline changes. (This
# replaces a static sentence -- "fiction, poetry and short-stories" --
# that survived two later, real fixes to the underlying data unnoticed,
# because nothing forced it to be re-checked against the actual numbers.)
#
# "Meets or beats Stonybrook" is measured against BestOverall, not
# BestPerGenre: BestOverall is Stonybrook's own single, one-classifier-
# across-every-genre result, the fair like-for-like comparison against
# this vignette's own single pooled GLMNET classifier. BestPerGenre
# reflects the best of 15 separately genre-tuned models, which isn't a
# fair comparison to one model's per-genre breakdown.
non_all <- comparisonTable %>% filter(Genre != 'all')
meets_or_beats <- non_all %>% filter(GLMNET >= BestOverall) %>% pull(Genre)
underperforms <- non_all %>%
  filter(GLMNET < BestOverall) %>%
  arrange(GLMNET - BestOverall) %>%
  pull(Genre)

meets_sentence <- if (length(meets_or_beats) > 0) {
  paste0(
    length(meets_or_beats), " of ", nrow(non_all), " genres -- ",
    paste(meets_or_beats, collapse = ", "),
    " -- meet or exceed Stonybrook's single best-overall classifier's result for that genre."
  )
} else {
  "No genre currently meets Stonybrook's single best-overall classifier's result for that genre."
}

underperform_sentence <- if (length(underperforms) > 0) {
  worst_n <- non_all$n[non_all$Genre == underperforms[1]]
  paste0(
    "The remaining ", length(underperforms), " underperform, with **", underperforms[1],
    "** showing the largest gap (n = ", worst_n, ").",
    if (worst_n < small_sample_threshold) {
      paste0(" That genre's test set is small enough (fewer than ", small_sample_threshold,
             " books) that this gap should be treated cautiously rather than as a settled finding.")
    } else {
      ""
    }
  )
} else {
  ""
}

cat(meets_sentence, underperform_sentence)
```
